title: The flying Sikh
hook: Milkha Singh, a Partition orphan, became a famous sprinter

segments.voice: Yesterday, nimrata, and your line was quiet service. Today, a man who was anything but quiet on a running track.

Running came into Milkha Singh's life long before any race. In the violence of Partition, by his own telling, a boy ran for his life while his village was attacked behind him. He lost his parents and others of his family, and arrived in Delhi a refugee with nothing. Years later the same boy would be running again, on cinder tracks, in front of crowds, with a nickname that followed him for the rest of his life. Today: the flying Sikh.
screen: `A BOY RUNNING FOR HIS LIFE.` → `A REFUGEE WITH NOTHING.` → `THE FLYING SIKH.`

segments.voice: First, the loss. In his autobiography, Milkha Singh describes Partition taking his parents and others he loved, and the hunger and drifting that came after, in camps and on city streets. He doesn't make it pretty. Second, the army. He joined the Indian Army, and there, he says, he found out he could run: a race for soldiers, a reward of extra milk, then more races, then training he describes as brutal and lonely. A body that had run for its life learned to run for something else. Third, the race in Pakistan. He tells how he was invited to race in Lahore, across the new border, in the land where his family had been killed. At first he refused. He was persuaded, ran, and won, and in his telling that's where he was called the flying Sikh. The name came from the other side of the line. Fourth, the root. In Gujri ki Var, at Ang 522 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says: keep making the effort, and you will live; keep working, and you will taste peace; keep remembering the Lord, and worry falls away. It doesn't say loss is good, or that Partition was a gift. It says the next step is still yours to take. Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits that keep climbing even after loss. His story doesn't erase what he lost. It shows what he ran toward anyway.
screen: `A FAMILY LOST AT PARTITION.` · `THE ARMY, AND A RACE FOR MILK.` · `A RACE ACROSS THE NEW BORDER.` · `KEEP MAKING THE EFFORT.` · then, large: `FROM ORPHAN TO ATHLETE.`

segments.voice: Sit with both feet flat on the floor and press them down gently, feeling your legs wake up. Breathe in and remember a time you ran or walked fast just for the joy of it; breathe out and bring to mind one hard thing you carried forward instead of leaving behind, and let the two sit side by side. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each breath.
Milkha Singh. The runner who lost his parents at Partition, found his speed in the army, and was given the name the flying Sikh after a race in Lahore. Today's word.
Your line: from orphan to athlete. The loss was real, and so was the next stride. That's day one thousand nineteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits even after loss, and stories like Milkha Singh's are told in families and gurdwaras as examples of carrying on after Partition.
